notes.front: What is an investment company?
notes.back: A company or fund that pools money from many investors and invests it primarily in securities.
notes.explanation: Each share represents part ownership of the fund’s investments and the income they generate.
notes.example: A fund that collects savings from thousands of people and buys a portfolio of stocks and bonds with it.
notes.evidence: A company or fund that pools money from many investors and invests that money primarily in securities. Each investment company share represents an investor’s part ownership in the fund’s underlying investments and the income those investments generate.

notes.front: What is a face-amount certificate company under the Investment Company Act?
notes.back: An investment company in the business of issuing face-amount certificates of the installment type, or with such certificates still outstanding.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Act’s three principal classes of investment company.
notes.example: A company selling certificates bought by instalments that promise a stated sum later.
notes.evidence: "Face-amount certificate company" means an investment company which is engaged or proposes to engage in the business of issuing face-amount certificates of the installment type, or which has been engaged in such business and has any such certificate outstanding.

notes.front: How does the Investment Company Act define a unit investment trust (UIT)?
notes.back: An investment company organised under a trust indenture or similar, with no board of directors, issuing only redeemable interests in a unit of specified securities.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Act’s three principal classes of investment company.
notes.example: A trust that buys 20 named bonds once and sells redeemable units in that fixed basket.
notes.evidence: "Unit investment trust" means an investment company which (A) is organized under a trust indenture, contract of custodianship or agency, or similar instrument, (B) does not have a board of directors, and (C) issues only redeemable securities, each of which represents an undivided interest in a unit of specified securities

notes.front: What is a management company under the Investment Company Act?
notes.back: Any investment company other than a face-amount certificate company or a unit investment trust.
notes.explanation: It is the third principal class, defined by exclusion.
notes.example: A mutual fund with a board and an adviser who trades its portfolio.
notes.evidence: "Management company" means any investment company other than a face-amount certificate company or a unit investment trust.

notes.front: What is an open-end fund (open-end company) under the Investment Company Act?
notes.back: A management company that is offering for sale or has outstanding any redeemable security of which it is the issuer.
notes.explanation: Mutual funds are open-end funds.
notes.example: A mutual fund that sells new shares daily and buys them back on request.
notes.evidence: "Open-end company" means a management company which is offering for sale or has outstanding any redeemable security of which it is the issuer.

notes.front: What is a closed-end fund (closed-end company) under the Investment Company Act?
notes.back: Any management company other than an open-end company.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov notes closed-end funds often sell a fixed number of shares at one time, which later trade on secondary markets.
notes.example: Like a mutual fund, but it sells a fixed batch of shares once and investors then trade them on an exchange.
notes.evidence: "Closed-end company" means any management company other than an open-end company.

notes.front: What is a diversified company under the Investment Company Act?
notes.back: A management company with at least 75% of total assets in cash, Government securities, other investment companies and securities limited per issuer.
notes.explanation: Each issuer is limited to 5% of the company’s total assets and 10% of the issuer’s voting securities.
notes.example: A stock fund spreading its assets so no single company is a large slice.
notes.evidence: "Diversified company" means a management company which meets the following requirements: At least 75 per centum of the value of its total assets is represented by cash and cash items (including receivables), Government securities, securities of other investment companies, and other securities

notes.front: What is a variable annuity?
notes.back: An annuity contract with an insurance company that is a security; its value varies with the investment options chosen, often mutual funds.
notes.explanation: Because it is a security, it is regulated by the SEC; poor performance can lose you money.
notes.example: A contract with an insurer whose value rises and falls with the stock funds you pick inside it.
notes.evidence: A variable annuity is a type of annuity contract between you and an insurance company that is a security and therefore regulated by the SEC. A variable annuity offers a range of investment options, often a menu of mutual funds.

notes.front: What is a fixed annuity?
notes.back: An insurance product promising a minimum interest rate while the account grows, and periodic payments of a set amount for a fixed or indefinite period.
notes.explanation: The insurer guarantees both the minimum rate and the payment amount.
notes.example: Like a variable annuity, but with a guaranteed minimum rate instead of fund-linked returns.
notes.evidence: An insurance product that promises a minimum rate of interest while your account is growing. The insurance company also guarantees that the periodic payment will be for a set amount for a fixed period, such as 20 years, or an indefinite period, such as your lifetime.

notes.front: What is a sales charge (sales load, or load) on a mutual fund?
notes.back: A fee investors pay when they buy (front-end) or redeem (back-end) mutual fund shares, similar to a commission.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov treats sales charge, sales load and load as the same thing.
notes.example: Paying a fund a percentage of your purchase, much like a broker’s commission.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Sales Charge or Sales Load”
notes.evidence: A sales charge, also called a sales load or load, is a fee investors pay when they buy (front-end sales load) or redeem (back-end sales load) shares in a mutual fund, similar to a commission.

notes.front: What is a front-end load?
notes.back: An upfront fee paid when buying mutual fund shares, deducted from the purchase so less money buys shares.
notes.explanation: Funds typically use it to compensate the brokers who sell their shares.
notes.example: Investing $1,000 with a 5% front-end load: $50 goes to the charge, $950 buys shares.
notes.evidence: A front-end sales load, also called a front-end load or front-end sales charge, is an upfront fee investors pay when they buy mutual fund shares. Funds typically use these fees to compensate brokers who sell the fund’s shares.

notes.front: What is a contingent deferred sales charge (CDSC)?
notes.back: The most common back-end sales load: a fee paid when selling fund shares back, which depends on how long they were held.
notes.explanation: It may gradually decline to zero if the shares are held long enough.
notes.example: Like a front-end load, but charged on the way out and shrinking the longer you stay.
notes.evidence: Also referred to as a Contingent Deferred Sales Charge (CDSC), this is the most common type of back-end sales load—a fee investors pay when they sell mutual fund shares back to the fund. The amount of this type of fee depends on the length of time the investor holds his or her shares.

notes.front: What is a mutual fund share class?
notes.back: One of several types of shares a single fund issues (Class A, Class B…): same investments, but different fees and expenses.
notes.explanation: So each class has different performance results.
notes.example: Class A and Class C shares of one fund, owning the same stocks but charging differently.
notes.evidence: Some mutual funds offer investors different types of shares, known as "classes." Different types of shares issued by a single fund are sometimes referred to as Class A shares, Class B shares, and so on.

notes.front: What is an investment company’s net asset value (NAV)?
notes.back: Its total assets minus its total liabilities.
notes.explanation: Per-share NAV divides this by the number of shares outstanding.
notes.example: A fund holding $200 million of assets and owing $20 million has a NAV of $180 million.
notes.evidence: "Net asset value," or "NAV," of an investment company is the company's total assets minus its total liabilities.

notes.front: What is a fund’s expense ratio?
notes.back: The percentage of the fund’s average net assets used each year to pay its operating expenses.
notes.explanation: It can include management fees, 12b-1 fees and other expenses, and appears in the prospectus fee table.
notes.example: A fund with a 0.50% expense ratio spends $5 a year per $1,000 of average net assets on running costs.
notes.evidence: The percentage of a fund's average net assets used each year to pay the fund’s operating expenses, which can include management fees, distribution and/or service fees (called 12b-1 fees), acquired fund fees and expenses, and other expenses.

notes.front: What is a 12b-1 fee?
notes.back: A fee paid out of fund assets to cover distribution costs and sometimes shareholder services.
notes.explanation: It is named after the SEC rule that authorises a fund to charge it.
notes.example: Part of a fund’s assets going each year to pay brokers and print sales literature.
notes.evidence: So-called “12b-1 fees” are fees paid out of fund assets to cover the costs of distribution and sometimes shareholder services

notes.front: What is a breakpoint?
notes.back: An investment level at which a fund with a front-end load charges a lower sales load.
notes.explanation: Some funds with front-end loads charge lower loads for larger investments.
notes.example: A load that drops from 5% to 4% once a purchase reaches $50,000.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: Some mutual funds that charge front-end sales loads will charge lower sales loads for larger investments.

notes.front: What is a right of accumulation (ROA)?
notes.back: A breakpoint discount given when the dollar amount of purchased shares, possibly combined with existing holdings, reaches a set threshold.
notes.explanation: Some funds count a household’s holdings; others only the individual’s.
notes.example: Adding a $20,000 purchase to $40,000 already held to reach a $50,000 breakpoint.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: some funds offer a breakpoint discount when the dollar amount of purchased shares reaches or surpasses a pre-determined threshold, or a “rights of accumulation” breakpoint.

notes.front: What is a letter of intent (LOI) in mutual fund purchases?
notes.back: A signed pledge to make additional purchases in future, which lets the investor get a breakpoint discount now.
notes.explanation: Failing to honour the pledge may bring retroactive fees that rescind the discount.
notes.example: Buying $30,000 now and pledging a further $20,000 later to get the $50,000 breakpoint today.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: some funds permit investors to obtain a breakpoint discount if the investors agree to make additional purchases in the future. In such cases, the investor signs a letter of intent to make additional purchases in the future.

notes.front: What is a surrender charge on a variable annuity?
notes.back: A fee for withdrawing money within a set period (the surrender period), such as six to ten years, after each premium payment.
notes.explanation: It decreases each year until it reaches zero.
notes.example: A 6% fee for cashing out a variable annuity in its second year.
notes.evidence: A type of transaction fee that applies if you withdraw some or all of your money from a variable annuity within a certain period of time, such as six to ten years, following each premium payment invested in the contract.

notes.front: What is a 529 plan?
notes.back: A tax-advantaged savings plan for certain education costs, legally a “qualified tuition plan”, sponsored by states, state agencies or educational institutions.
notes.explanation: It is authorised by Section 529 of the Internal Revenue Code.
notes.example: A grandparent saving for a grandchild’s university costs in a state-sponsored plan.
notes.evidence: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged savings plan designed to encourage saving for certain educational costs. 529 plans, legally known as “qualified tuition plans,” are sponsored by states, state agencies, or educational institutions and are authorized by Section 529 of the Internal Revenue Code.

notes.front: What is a prepaid tuition plan?
notes.back: A type of 529 plan in which the account owner buys units or credits at participating colleges for the beneficiary’s future tuition.
notes.explanation: It pays for tuition in advance rather than investing for growth.
notes.example: Buying a year of tuition credits at a state university for a child now aged six.
notes.evidence: A type of 529 plan that lets an account owner purchase units or credits at participating colleges or universities for future tuition for the account beneficiary.

notes.front: What is a 529 savings plan?
notes.back: One of the two basic types of 529 plan, alongside prepaid tuition plans; states may offer both.
notes.explanation: The IRS notes that an educational institution can offer only the prepaid type.
notes.example: Like a prepaid tuition plan, but the money is invested rather than buying tuition credits.
notes.evidence: There are two basic types: prepaid tuition plans and savings plans. And each state has its own plan. Each is somewhat unique. States are permitted to offer both types. A qualified education institution can only offer a prepaid tuition type 529 plan.

notes.front: Who is a 529 account owner?
notes.back: The person who opens the account for a student to save for qualifying education expenses; also called the account holder or saver.
notes.explanation: The account is opened for someone else: the student.
notes.example: A parent who opens and funds a 529 account for her son.
notes.evidence: A person who establishes an account for a student to save money for qualified higher education expenses or tuition for elementary or secondary public, private, or religious schools; also called the account holder or the saver.

notes.front: Who is the designated beneficiary of a 529 account?
notes.back: The current or future student for whom the account is established.
notes.explanation: The IRS notes each 529 account has one designated beneficiary.
notes.example: The son whose future tuition his mother’s 529 account will pay.
notes.evidence: A current or future student for whom the 529 account is established.

notes.front: What are qualified education expenses for a 529 plan?
notes.back: Costs such as tuition, fees, books and room and board at an eligible institution, plus some elementary or secondary school costs.
notes.explanation: Earnings used for them escape federal tax.
notes.example: A university’s tuition bill and required textbooks, paid from the 529 account.
notes.evidence: when used for the qualified education expenses of the designated beneficiary, such as tuition, fees, books, as well as room and board at an eligible education institution and tuition at elementary or secondary schools.

notes.front: What is an ABLE account?
notes.back: A tax-advantaged savings account states may create for eligible people with disabilities; distributions are tax-free if used for qualified disability expenses.
notes.explanation: It was created by the Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act of 2014.
notes.example: A young adult with a disability saving for housing and transport costs.
notes.source: IRS, “ABLE accounts – Tax benefit for people with disabilities”
notes.evidence: The Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act of 2014 allows states to create tax-advantaged savings programs for eligible people with disabilities (designated beneficiaries). Funds from these 529A ABLE accounts can help designated beneficiaries pay for qualified disability expenses. Distributions are tax-free if used for qualified disability expenses.

notes.front: How does SEC Rule 3a12-9 define a direct participation program (DPP)?
notes.back: A program financed by selling securities that are not exchange-listed or actively traded, and that gives investors flow-through tax consequences.
notes.explanation: The rule excludes REITs and registered investment companies, among others.
notes.example: An unlisted oil-drilling partnership whose income and deductions flow to its investors’ tax returns.
notes.evidence: a program financed through the sale of securities, other than securities that are listed on an exchange, quoted on NASDAQ, or will otherwise be actively traded during the pay-in period as a result of efforts by the issuer, underwriter, or other participants in the initial distribution of such securities, that provides for flow-through tax consequences to its investors

notes.front: How is a limited partnership run, as the SEC describes master limited partnerships?
notes.back: A general partner manages its affairs, with no board of directors of its own; others hold limited partner interests.
notes.explanation: The SEC notes a sponsor can control the partnership by controlling its general partner.
notes.example: An energy partnership managed by one firm, with thousands of outside investors holding units.
notes.source: SEC Updated Investor Bulletin: Master Limited Partnerships – An Introduction (3 November 2017)
notes.evidence: The GP manages the affairs of the MLP; the MLP does not have a board of directors of its own. In addition to holding the general partner interests of the MLP, the sponsor also holds limited partner interests

notes.front: What is the general partner’s role in a limited partnership?
notes.back: It manages the partnership’s affairs.
notes.explanation: In the SEC’s description of master limited partnerships, the general partner runs the business and the partnership has no board of directors of its own.
notes.example: The operating company that runs a partnership’s pipelines day to day.
notes.source: SEC Updated Investor Bulletin: Master Limited Partnerships – An Introduction (3 November 2017)
notes.evidence: The GP manages the affairs of the MLP; the MLP does not have a board of directors of its own.

notes.front: What is a limited partner?
notes.back: An investor who buys limited partner interests (units); liability for the partnership’s debts generally extends only up to capital contributed.
notes.explanation: This is the limited liability of partnership investors.
notes.example: Like a general partner’s co-owner, but not managing and with capped exposure to debts.
notes.source: SEC Updated Investor Bulletin: Master Limited Partnerships – An Introduction (3 November 2017)
notes.evidence: Investors may become limited partners in an MLP by purchasing limited partner interests, known as units. Although the limited partners are liable for the debts and obligations of the MLP, each limited partner’s liability generally extends only up to the amount of capital contributed.

notes.front: What is pass-through tax treatment of a partnership?
notes.back: The partnership itself pays no income tax; its partners are liable for income tax individually.
notes.explanation: 26 U.S.C. 701 puts the tax on the partners, not the partnership.
notes.example: A partnership earns $1 million; it files no tax bill, and each partner pays tax on their share.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. 701 (partners, not partnership, subject to tax)
notes.evidence: A partnership as such shall not be subject to the income tax imposed by this chapter. Persons carrying on business as partners shall be liable for income tax only in their separate or individual capacities.

notes.front: What is a real estate investment trust (REIT)?
notes.back: A company that owns and typically operates income-producing real estate or related assets, such as offices, apartments or mortgages.
notes.explanation: It lets individuals invest in large-scale, income-producing real estate.
notes.example: A listed company owning 40 shopping centres and collecting their rents.
notes.evidence: A REIT is a company that owns and typically operates income-producing real estate or related assets. These may include office buildings, shopping malls, apartments, hotels, resorts, self-storage facilities, warehouses, and mortgages or loans.

notes.front: What is a non-traded REIT?
notes.back: A REIT that is registered with the SEC and files regular reports, but is not listed on an exchange or publicly traded.
notes.explanation: The SEC says it poses risks different from a publicly traded REIT.
notes.example: Like a listed REIT, but you cannot sell its shares on a stock exchange.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Non-traded REITs (31 August 2015)
notes.evidence: there are also non-traded REITs that are registered with the SEC, file regular reports with the SEC, but are not listed on an exchange and are not publicly traded.

notes.front: What is a hedge fund?
notes.back: A private, unregistered investment fund that pools investors’ money; generally limited to individuals and institutions meeting financial or sophistication criteria.
notes.explanation: Its aim is positive returns from securities or other assets.
notes.example: A private fund for wealthy investors that borrows and sells short to profit in rising and falling markets.
notes.evidence: A hedge fund is a private, unregistered investment fund. Hedge funds pool money from investors and invest in securities or other types of assets with the goal of getting positive returns. Hedge funds are generally limited to individuals and institutional investors who meet certain financial or sophistication criteria.

notes.front: What is a private equity fund?
notes.back: A pooled fund managed by a private equity firm, often focused on long-term investments in assets that take time to sell.
notes.explanation: Its investment horizon is typically 10 or more years.
notes.example: A fund that buys control of a family-owned manufacturer, improves it and sells it a decade later.
notes.evidence: Unlike mutual funds or hedge funds, however, private equity firms often focus on long-term investment opportunities in assets that take time to sell with an investment time horizon typically of 10 or more years.

notes.front: What is an exchange-traded product (ETP)?
notes.back: An investment product listed and traded on a national securities exchange, such as an exchange-traded fund, commodity trust or note.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov says exchange-traded funds are the most common type.
notes.example: Any fund or note you can buy through a broker on a stock exchange during the day.
notes.evidence: Exchange-traded products (ETPs) are investment products that are listed and traded on national securities exchanges. These investment products include exchange-traded funds, exchange-traded commodity trusts and exchange-traded notes (ETNs).

notes.front: What is an exchange-traded fund (ETF)?
notes.back: An exchange-traded investment product that must register with the SEC as an open-end investment company (or sometimes a unit investment trust).
notes.explanation: Like mutual funds, ETFs pool investors’ money and invest it in securities.
notes.example: Like a mutual fund, but bought and sold on an exchange at market prices.
notes.evidence: An ETF is an exchange-traded investment product that must register with the SEC as an open-end investment company (or sometimes as a unit investment trust).

notes.front: What is an exchange-traded note (ETN)?
notes.back: An unsecured debt obligation of a financial institution, traded on an exchange, whose payments are linked to a reference index or benchmark.
notes.explanation: The SEC warns ETNs are complex and can lose the entire investment.
notes.example: A bank’s 30-year note, traded on an exchange, that pays whatever a commodity index returns, less fees.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Exchange Traded Notes (ETNs) (1 December 2015)
notes.evidence: ETNs are unsecured debt obligations of financial institutions that trade on a securities exchange. ETN payment terms are linked to the performance of a reference index or benchmark, representing the ETN’s investment objective.

notes.front: What is an actively managed fund?
notes.back: A mutual fund or ETF relying on an adviser’s skill to build and manage its portfolio, seeking certain exposures or to beat a benchmark.
notes.explanation: The adviser may trade without regard to conformity with an index.
notes.example: A fund whose manager picks 40 stocks she expects to beat the market.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Active Fund or Actively Managed Fund”
notes.evidence: An active, or actively managed, mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) follows an investment strategy that relies on the skill of an investment adviser to construct and manage its portfolio in an effort to provide exposure to certain types of investments or outperform an investment benchmark or index.

notes.front: What is an index fund?
notes.back: A mutual fund, ETF or UIT following a passive strategy designed to achieve approximately the same return as a particular index, before fees.
notes.explanation: It invests mainly in the securities included in the chosen index.
notes.example: Like an actively managed fund, but simply holding the stocks in a market index.
notes.evidence: These funds follow a passive investment strategy designed to achieve approximately the same return as a particular index before fees.

notes.front: Under Investment Company Act s. 3(a)(1)(C), what share of total assets in investment securities can make a securities business an investment company?
notes.back: More than 40% (excluding Government securities and cash items), measured on an unconsolidated basis.
notes.explanation: This is one of the Act’s three tests of an investment company.
notes.evidence: owns or proposes to acquire investment securities having a value exceeding 40 per centum of the value of such issuer's total assets (exclusive of Government securities and cash items)

notes.front: Open-end funds, closed-end funds and UITs: how does each offer its shares?
notes.back: Open-end: continuously. Closed-end: often a fixed number at once, later traded. UIT: one-time offering of a fixed number of units.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov calls these the three basic types of investment company.
notes.evidence: Open-end investment companies or open-end funds —which sell shares on a continuous basis

notes.front: A registered fund has a board of directors and issues redeemable shares; it is not a trust and issues no face-amount certificates. Which Investment Company Act class is it?
notes.back: C: a management company.
notes.choices:
A) Unit investment trust
B) Face-amount certificate company
C) Management company
notes.choicesExplained: A: a UIT has no board of directors. B: it issues no face-amount certificates.
notes.explanation: A management company is any investment company that is neither of the other two.
notes.evidence: "Management company" means any investment company other than a face-amount certificate company or a unit investment trust.

notes.front: A fund is organised under a trust indenture, has no board of directors and issues only redeemable units in a set basket of bonds. Which class is it?
notes.back: A: a unit investment trust.
notes.choices:
A) Unit investment trust
B) Closed-end fund
C) Face-amount certificate company
notes.choicesExplained: B: a closed-end fund is a management company, which a board-less trust is not. C: it issues no face-amount certificates.
notes.explanation: Trust instrument, no board and only redeemable units define a UIT.
notes.evidence: (A) is organized under a trust indenture, contract of custodianship or agency, or similar instrument, (B) does not have a board of directors, and (C) issues only redeemable securities

notes.front: Who manages a UIT’s portfolio during its life?
notes.back: No one actively: a UIT has no board, corporate officers or investment adviser, and holds a fixed portfolio with little or no change.
notes.explanation: Investors therefore know roughly what they hold for the whole investment.
notes.evidence: A UIT does not have a board of directors, corporate officers, or an investment adviser to render advice during the life of the trust.

notes.front: How can a UIT investor get out before the trust ends?
notes.back: Redeem the units with the UIT at approximately NAV, or sell in a secondary market if the sponsor maintains one.
notes.explanation: UIT units are redeemable, like mutual fund shares.
notes.evidence: A UIT typically issues redeemable units, like a mutual fund. This means that the UIT will buy back an investor’s units at their approximate net asset value (or NAV ). Many UIT sponsors, however, will also maintain a secondary market

notes.front: Mutual fund (open-end) vs publicly traded closed-end fund: which must buy back shares from shareholders?
notes.back: Only the open-end fund; closed-end funds are not required to, and their shares trade on exchanges at market prices.
notes.explanation: The closed-end market price may be above or below the value of its holdings.
notes.evidence: Unlike traditional mutual funds (or “open-end funds”), they are not required to buy back shares from shareholders.

notes.front: At what price can a mutual fund investor sell shares back to the fund?
notes.back: The next calculated NAV, minus any fees charged at redemption.
notes.explanation: Mutual fund shares are redeemable on any business day.
notes.evidence: Mutual fund shares are redeemable. This means investors can sell the shares back to the fund at any time at the next calculated NAV, minus any fees charged at the time of redemption.

notes.front: A fund sold 10 million shares in an initial public offering; the shares now trade on an exchange and the fund does not redeem them. What is it?
notes.back: B: a closed-end fund.
notes.choices:
A) An open-end fund
B) A closed-end fund
C) A 529 plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: an open-end fund sells shares continuously and redeems them. C: a 529 plan is an education savings plan, not an investment company whose shares trade on an exchange.
notes.explanation: Closed-end funds often sell a fixed number of shares once, which then trade on secondary markets.
notes.evidence: Closed-end investment companies or closed-end funds —which often sell a fixed number of shares at one time (in an initial public offering) that later trade on secondary markets

notes.front: In a diversified company’s 75% test, securities of any one issuer count only up to {{c1::5 per cent}} of the company’s total assets.
notes.explanation: The same test also caps holdings at 10% of the issuer’s voting securities.
notes.evidence: limited in respect of any one issuer to an amount not greater in value than 5 per centum of the value of the total assets of such management company

notes.front: In a diversified company’s 75% test, holdings of any one issuer count only up to {{c1::10 per cent}} of that issuer’s outstanding voting securities.
notes.explanation: The same test also caps each issuer at 5% of the company’s total assets.
notes.evidence: and to not more than 10 per centum of the outstanding voting securities of such issuer.

notes.front: What is a non-diversified company under the Investment Company Act?
notes.back: Any management company other than a diversified company.
notes.explanation: The Act splits management companies into diversified and non-diversified.
notes.evidence: "Non-diversified company" means any management company other than a diversified company.

notes.front: A management company has only 70% of its total assets in cash, Government securities and securities meeting the per-issuer limits. How is it classed?
notes.back: B: non-diversified.
notes.choices:
A) Diversified
B) Non-diversified
C) A unit investment trust
notes.choicesExplained: A: a diversified company needs at least 75% in qualifying assets. C: a UIT is a separate class, not a management company.
notes.explanation: It fails the 75% test, so it is any management company other than a diversified one.
notes.evidence: At least 75 per centum of the value of its total assets is represented by cash and cash items (including receivables), Government securities, securities of other investment companies, and other securities

notes.front: How are gains inside a variable annuity taxed?
notes.back: Tax-deferred: no federal tax on income and gains until a withdrawal, income payment or death benefit is paid.
notes.explanation: Moving money between investment options inside the contract is not taxed at the time.
notes.evidence: Second , variable annuities are tax-deferred . That means you pay no federal taxes on the income and investment gains from your annuity until you make a withdrawal, receive income payments, or a death benefit is paid.

notes.front: What does a variable annuity’s standard death benefit generally pay the beneficiary?
notes.back: The greater of the account value or a guaranteed minimum, such as purchase payments minus prior withdrawals.
notes.explanation: It is a common feature during the accumulation phase.
notes.evidence: If you die, a person you select as a beneficiary (such as your spouse or child) will generally receive the greater of: (i) all the money in your account; or (ii) some guaranteed minimum (such as all purchase payments minus prior withdrawals).

notes.front: What two costs may hit a withdrawal from a variable annuity in its early years before age 59½?
notes.back: Surrender charges; and a 10% federal tax penalty.
notes.explanation: The SEC names both for early withdrawals during accumulation.
notes.evidence: if you withdraw money from your account during the early years of the accumulation phase, you may have to pay “surrender charges” (discussed below). In addition, you may have to pay a 10% federal tax penalty if you withdraw money before the age of 59½.

notes.front: A client wants somewhere to park money for a house purchase in 18 months. Is a variable annuity suitable?
notes.back: B: variable annuities are not suitable for short-term goals.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: it is tax-deferred
B) No: variable annuities are not suitable for short-term goals
C) Yes, if she picks bond funds inside it
notes.choicesExplained: A: despite tax deferral, the SEC says variable annuities are not suitable for short-term goals. C: the fund choice does not remove surrender charges and taxes on early withdrawal.
notes.explanation: Substantial taxes and surrender charges may apply to early withdrawals.
notes.evidence: Variable annuities are not suitable for meeting short-term goals. Substantial taxes and surrender charges may apply if you withdraw your money early.

notes.front: When exchanging one variable annuity for another, what surrender-charge costs may arise?
notes.back: Surrender charges on the old contract if still in its period, and a new surrender period on the new one.
notes.explanation: The SEC advises comparing the two contracts first.
notes.evidence: If you exchange contracts, you may be required to pay surrender charges on the old annuity if you are still in the surrender charge period. In addition, a new surrender charge period may begin when you exchange into the new annuity.

notes.front: Fixed annuity vs variable annuity: who regulates each?
notes.back: Fixed: an insurance product regulated by state insurance regulators. Variable: also a security, so registered with the SEC too.
notes.explanation: A variable annuity is both an insurance product and a security.
notes.evidence: An insurance product. Regulated by state insurance regulator. Contact the State insurance commission An insurance product. Regulated by state insurance regulator. Contact the State insurance commission An insurance product and a security. Regulated by state insurance regulator and registered with the SEC.

notes.front: A retiree’s annuity lets her choose among stock and bond mutual funds, and its value moves with their performance. What does she own?
notes.back: B: a variable annuity.
notes.choices:
A) A fixed annuity
B) A variable annuity
C) A unit investment trust
notes.choicesExplained: A: a fixed annuity promises a minimum rate rather than fund-linked value. C: a UIT is an investment company with a fixed portfolio, not an insurance contract.
notes.explanation: A variable annuity’s value varies with the investment options chosen.
notes.evidence: The value of your contract will vary depending on the performance of the investment options you choose. If they perform poorly, you could lose money.

notes.front: An investor puts $20,000 into a fund with a 4% front-end load. How much buys shares?
notes.explanation: The load is deducted from the purchase before shares are bought.
notes.evidence: A front-end sales load is deducted from the purchase and reduces the amount available to buy fund shares.

notes.front: Front-end load vs CDSC: when is each paid?
notes.back: Front-end load: when buying. CDSC: when selling shares back, depending on how long they were held.
notes.explanation: Both are sales loads, taken at opposite ends of the investment.
notes.evidence: a fee investors pay when they sell mutual fund shares back to the fund. The amount of this type of fee depends on the length of time the investor holds his or her shares.

notes.front: Do different share classes of one fund hold different investments?
notes.back: No: all classes hold identical investments with the same objectives; only fees and expenses, and so performance, differ.
notes.explanation: A multi-class structure lets investors choose a fee structure that suits them.
notes.evidence: All classes of a fund hold identical investments and have the same investment objectives and policies. But each class has different fees and expenses, and therefore, each class will have different performance results.

notes.front: A fund has $50 million of assets, $5 million of liabilities and 3 million shares outstanding. What is its per-share NAV?
notes.explanation: Per-share NAV is NAV divided by the shares outstanding.
notes.evidence: An investment company calculates the NAV of a single share (or the "per share NAV") by dividing its NAV by the number of shares that are outstanding.

notes.front: How often must mutual funds and UITs generally calculate NAV, and does the rule cover closed-end funds?
notes.back: At least once every business day, typically after the major exchanges close; closed-end funds are not subject to it.
notes.explanation: Closed-end fund shares generally are not redeemable.
notes.evidence: Mutual funds and Unit Investment Trusts (UITs) generally must calculate their NAV at least once every business day, typically after the major U.S. exchanges close. A closed-end fund , whose shares generally are not "redeemable"—that is, not required to be repurchased by the fund—is not subject to this requirement.

notes.front: A fund’s per-share NAV is $19.00 and it adds a front-end sales load of $1.00 a share. What does an investor pay per share?
notes.back: $20.00: NAV plus the load imposed at purchase.
notes.explanation: The purchase price is approximately NAV plus fees imposed at purchase.
notes.evidence: the price that investors pay to purchase mutual fund and most UIT shares is the approximate per share NAV, plus any fees that the fund imposes at purchase

notes.front: What are the two kinds of mutual fund prospectus?
notes.back: The statutory (long-form) prospectus and the summary prospectus, a few pages of key information.
notes.explanation: The same key information must open the statutory prospectus.
notes.evidence: There are two kinds of prospectuses: (1) the statutory prospectus; and (2) the summary prospectus.

notes.front: A fund’s average net assets are $400 million and its annual operating expenses $3 million. What is its expense ratio?
notes.explanation: The ratio is expenses as a percentage of average net assets.
notes.evidence: The percentage of a fund's average net assets used each year to pay the fund’s operating expenses

notes.front: What do the two kinds of 12b-1 fee pay for?
notes.back: Distribution fees: marketing and selling shares. Shareholder service fees: people who answer investor inquiries.
notes.explanation: Shareholder service fees can also be paid outside 12b-1 fees.
notes.evidence: Distribution fees cover the marketing and selling of fund shares, such as compensating brokers and others who sell fund shares.

notes.front: Typically, 12b-1 fees apply to mutual funds but not to {{c1::ETFs}}.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov notes this typical pattern.
notes.evidence: Typically, 12b-1 fees apply to mutual funds but not to ETFs.

notes.front: Under Rule 12b-1, what must an open-end fund have before paying for distribution out of its assets?
notes.back: A written plan describing all material aspects of the proposed distribution financing, with related agreements in writing.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov notes the fees are named after this SEC rule.
notes.evidence: any payments made by such company in connection with such distribution are made pursuant to a written plan describing all material aspects of the proposed financing of distribution and that all agreements with any person relating to implementation of the plan are in writing

notes.front: Must funds offer breakpoint discounts, and what applies if they do?
notes.back: No; but if they do, funds must disclose them and brokers must apply them.
notes.explanation: Funds that offer them may set them at their discretion.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: Funds are not required to offer breakpoint discounts and those that do may set them at their discretion. But, if mutual funds offer breakpoints, mutual funds must disclose them and brokers must apply them.

notes.front: A fund’s breakpoint is $50,000. A broker suggests a client invest $49,500 so the broker earns a higher commission. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B: selling just below a breakpoint to earn more commission is not allowed.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the client agrees
B) No: firms may not sell just below a breakpoint simply to earn a higher commission
C) Yes, because breakpoints are optional
notes.choicesExplained: A: client agreement does not cure the practice. C: offering breakpoints is optional for funds, but brokers must apply those offered.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov says a brokerage firm may not sell fund shares just below a breakpoint simply to earn a higher commission.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: In addition, a brokerage firm is not allowed to sell shares of a mutual fund in an amount that is just below the mutual fund’s breakpoint simply to earn a higher commission.

notes.front: A fund charges 5.5% below $50,000 and 4.5% from $50,000. What load applies to a $60,000 purchase?
notes.back: 4.5%: the purchase passes the $50,000 breakpoint.
notes.explanation: Reaching the breakpoint earns the lower sales load.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: The investment levels required to obtain a reduced sales load are commonly referred to as breakpoints.

notes.front: For rights of accumulation, whose holdings may a fund count?
notes.back: It varies: some funds count a household’s total investments across accounts; others only what the individual holds.
notes.explanation: Each fund sets its own formula, so investors must ask.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: Some funds determine eligibility for this type of discount by looking at total investments in the fund by household, which may include multiple accounts, such as retirement savings accounts and college savings accounts. Other funds look only at the total amount that an individual has invested personally.

notes.front: A client already holds $35,000 in a fund and now buys $20,000 more. The fund’s breakpoint is $50,000 and it offers rights of accumulation. What may apply?
notes.back: A: the reduced load via rights of accumulation.
notes.choices:
A) The reduced load, since holdings plus purchase pass $50,000
B) The full load, since the new purchase alone is below $50,000
C) No load at all
notes.choicesExplained: B: rights of accumulation let the purchase combine with existing holdings. C: a breakpoint reduces the load; it need not remove it.
notes.explanation: Investors may be entitled to combine a purchase with existing holdings.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: Fund investors may also be entitled to combine a share purchase with existing holdings to obtain the discount.

notes.front: What may happen if an investor does not complete the purchases promised in a letter of intent?
notes.back: Retroactive fees may rescind the discount, and the fund may redeem shares from the account to recoup them.
notes.explanation: The discount depended on the promised future purchases.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: Failure to honor that pledge may result in retroactive fees that rescind the discount, and a fund might reserve the right to redeem shares from an investor’s account to recoup that amount.

notes.front: A client with no shares in a fund has $30,000 to invest now and firmly expects to add $25,000 next year. The breakpoint is $50,000. What lets her get the reduced load now?
notes.back: A: a letter of intent.
notes.choices:
A) A letter of intent
B) A right of accumulation
C) A 12b-1 plan
notes.choicesExplained: B: rights of accumulation count shares already bought; she holds none yet. C: a 12b-1 plan pays distribution costs and gives no discount.
notes.explanation: A letter of intent pledges future purchases to obtain the discount now.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Breakpoint Discounts or Sales Charge Discounts”
notes.evidence: some funds permit investors to obtain a breakpoint discount if the investors agree to make additional purchases in the future. In such cases, the investor signs a letter of intent to make additional purchases in the future.

notes.front: How does a variable annuity’s surrender charge change over time?
notes.back: It decreases each year until it reaches zero, but each new premium payment starts a new surrender period.
notes.explanation: So later payments carry their own charge schedule.
notes.evidence: The fee decreases each year until it becomes zero, although a new surrender charge period will begin with each new premium payment.

notes.front: A contract charges 7% in year one, falling 1% a year. What is the charge on a $10,000 withdrawal in year three?
notes.explanation: The charge declines gradually over the surrender period.
notes.evidence: For example, a 7% charge might apply in the first year after a purchase payment, 6% in the second year, 5% in the third year, and so on.

notes.front: What are the two types of 529 plan?
notes.back: Prepaid tuition plans and education savings plans.
notes.explanation: All 50 states and the District of Columbia sponsor at least one type.
notes.evidence: There are two types of 529 plans: prepaid tuition plans and education savings plans .

notes.front: The SEC {{c1::does not}} regulate or oversee 529 plans.
notes.explanation: States, state agencies or educational institutions sponsor them.
notes.evidence: The SEC does not regulate or oversee 529 Plans.

notes.front: What is the main tax advantage of a 529 plan, and are contributions deductible?
notes.back: Earnings escape federal tax (and generally state tax) when used for qualified education expenses; contributions are not deductible.
notes.explanation: The IRS calls this the main advantage of a typical plan.
notes.evidence: Earnings are not subject to federal tax and generally not subject to state tax when used for the qualified education expenses of the designated beneficiary

notes.front: From 2026, how much a year of elementary or secondary school expenses can a 529 plan pay as qualified expenses?
notes.back: Up to $20,000 a year (the limit was $10,000 from 2018 to 2025).
notes.explanation: A 2025 law doubled the annual limit for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. 529(e)(3)(A), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, section 70413(b)
notes.evidence: with respect to a beneficiary during any taxable year shall, in the aggregate, include not more than $20,000 in expenses described in subsection (c)(7) incurred during the taxable year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 26 U.S.C. 529 as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (taxable years from 2026)

notes.front: Can a 529 plan’s beneficiary be changed without tax?
notes.back: Yes, if the new designated beneficiary is another member of the family.
notes.explanation: Rollovers for the same beneficiary or a family member are also not taxable.
notes.evidence: There are no tax consequences if you change the designated beneficiary to another member of the family.

notes.front: Who controls the money in a 529 plan: the owner or the beneficiary?
notes.back: The owner: whoever buys the plan controls the funds until they are withdrawn.
notes.explanation: The beneficiary is the student the plan benefits.
notes.evidence: Whoever purchases the 529 plan is the custodian and controls the funds until they are withdrawn.

notes.front: A grandmother opens a 529 account for her granddaughter’s future college costs. Who is the account owner?
notes.back: A: the grandmother.
notes.choices:
A) The grandmother
B) The granddaughter
C) The college
notes.choicesExplained: B: the granddaughter is the designated beneficiary, the student the account is for. C: the college receives payments but has no role in the account.
notes.explanation: The owner establishes the account for a student.
notes.evidence: A person who establishes an account for a student to save money for qualified higher education expenses

notes.front: Prepaid tuition plan vs 529 savings plan: which can an educational institution offer on its own?
notes.back: Only the prepaid tuition type; states may offer either type.
notes.explanation: The IRS says each state has its own plan.
notes.evidence: States are permitted to offer both types. A qualified education institution can only offer a prepaid tuition type 529 plan.

notes.front: Parents want to buy tuition credits now at a participating university for their child’s future tuition. Which plan fits?
notes.back: A: a prepaid tuition plan.
notes.choices:
A) A prepaid tuition plan
B) An ABLE account
C) A variable annuity
notes.choicesExplained: B: an ABLE account saves for qualified disability expenses. C: a variable annuity is an insurance contract, not a tuition plan.
notes.explanation: Prepaid plans buy units or credits for future tuition.
notes.evidence: A type of 529 plan that lets an account owner purchase units or credits at participating colleges or universities for future tuition for the account beneficiary.

notes.front: Are ABLE account contributions federally deductible, and how are qualified withdrawals taxed?
notes.back: Not deductible; investments can grow tax-free and stay so when withdrawn for qualified disability expenses.
notes.explanation: The tax benefit is on growth, not contributions.
notes.evidence: Contributions are not tax deductible for federal income tax purposes, but your investments can grow tax free and remain so when withdrawn if used for qualified disability expenses.

notes.front: The SEC {{c1::does not}} regulate or oversee ABLE accounts.
notes.explanation: States create ABLE programs under federal tax law.
notes.evidence: The SEC does not regulate or oversee ABLE accounts.

notes.front: May money move from a 529 plan into an ABLE account?
notes.back: Yes, in limited amounts, into the ABLE account of the same beneficiary or a family member.
notes.explanation: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 added this rollover.
notes.source: IRS, “ABLE accounts – Tax benefit for people with disabilities”
notes.evidence: Funds from a designated beneficiary’s qualified tuition program (also known as a 529 plan) may be rolled into an ABLE account of the designated beneficiary or of his/her family member. The permissible rollover is limited in amount.

notes.front: A family wants a tax-advantaged account for a relative with a disability, to pay qualified disability expenses. Which fits?
notes.back: A: an ABLE account.
notes.choices:
A) An ABLE account
B) A prepaid tuition plan
C) A hedge fund
notes.choicesExplained: B: a prepaid tuition plan buys future tuition credits. C: a hedge fund is a private investment fund with no such tax status.
notes.explanation: ABLE accounts are tax-advantaged savings for eligible people with disabilities.
notes.source: IRS, “ABLE accounts – Tax benefit for people with disabilities”
notes.evidence: allows states to create tax-advantaged savings programs for eligible people with disabilities (designated beneficiaries).

notes.front: Under Rule 3a12-9, what are two things excluded from the term direct participation program?
notes.back: Any two of: REITs; Subchapter S offerings; tax-qualified pension and profit-sharing plans; IRAs; registered investment companies.
notes.explanation: The rule lists these exclusions expressly.
notes.evidence: the term “direct participation program” does not include real estate investment trusts, Subchapter S corporate offerings, tax qualified pension and profit sharing plans under sections 401 and 403(a) of the Internal Revenue Code (“Code”), tax shelter annuities under section 403(b) of the Code, individual retirement plans under section 408 of the Code

notes.front: Securities of a direct participation program are, by definition, {{c1::not listed on an exchange}} or otherwise actively traded during the pay-in period.
notes.explanation: Rule 3a12-9 defines the program by this and by flow-through tax treatment.
notes.evidence: other than securities that are listed on an exchange, quoted on NASDAQ, or will otherwise be actively traded during the pay-in period

notes.front: Which is a direct participation program under Rule 3a12-9?
notes.back: A: the unlisted partnership with flow-through tax treatment.
notes.choices:
A) An unlisted real estate partnership passing its income and losses to investors’ tax returns
B) A listed REIT
C) A registered mutual fund
notes.choicesExplained: B: REITs are expressly excluded. C: issuers registered under the Investment Company Act are excluded.
notes.explanation: The definition needs unlisted securities and flow-through tax consequences.
notes.evidence: that provides for flow-through tax consequences to its investors; Provided, however, That the term “direct participation program” does not include real estate investment trusts

notes.front: How do investors in a publicly traded partnership learn their share of its income, gains, losses and deductions?
notes.back: Each receives a Schedule K-1 every year.
notes.explanation: Limited partners report that share on their own returns.
notes.source: SEC Updated Investor Bulletin: Master Limited Partnerships – An Introduction (3 November 2017)
notes.evidence: Instead, limited partners report on their tax returns their share of the MLP’s income, gains, losses, and deductions, and are taxed at their individual tax rates. Each limited partner receives annually a Schedule K-1

notes.front: A partnership earns $2 million of taxable income this year. Who pays federal income tax on it?
notes.back: B: the partners, individually.
notes.choices:
A) The partnership itself
B) The partners, each on their own share
C) No one until the partnership is sold
notes.choicesExplained: A: a partnership as such is not subject to income tax. C: the Code puts the tax on the partners, with no wait for a sale.
notes.explanation: 26 U.S.C. 701 puts the tax on the partners.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. 701 (partners, not partnership, subject to tax)
notes.evidence: Persons carrying on business as partners shall be liable for income tax only in their separate or individual capacities.

notes.front: General partner vs limited partner: who manages the partnership, and whose liability is generally capped?
notes.back: The general partner manages; the limited partner’s liability generally extends only to capital contributed.
notes.explanation: The SEC describes both roles for master limited partnerships.
notes.source: SEC Updated Investor Bulletin: Master Limited Partnerships – An Introduction (3 November 2017)
notes.evidence: Although the limited partners are liable for the debts and obligations of the MLP, each limited partner’s liability generally extends only up to the amount of capital contributed.

notes.front: An investor bought $15,000 of units in a partnership as a limited partner. The partnership fails with large debts. Generally, what is her maximum exposure?
notes.back: A: generally up to her $15,000 contributed.
notes.choices:
A) $15,000, her capital contributed
B) Unlimited, like the general partner
C) Nothing, since limited partners are never liable
notes.choicesExplained: B: limited partners’ liability is generally capped. C: they are liable, but generally only up to capital contributed.
notes.explanation: A limited partner’s liability generally stops at the capital contributed.
notes.source: SEC Updated Investor Bulletin: Master Limited Partnerships – An Introduction (3 November 2017)
notes.evidence: each limited partner’s liability generally extends only up to the amount of capital contributed.

notes.front: How does a REIT differ from other real estate companies in what it does with properties?
notes.back: It does not develop properties to resell them; it buys and develops them to operate as part of its own portfolio.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov draws this line in its definition.
notes.evidence: Unlike other real estate companies, a REIT does not develop real estate properties to resell them. Instead, a REIT buys and develops properties primarily to operate them as part of its own investment portfolio.

notes.front: REITs have to distribute at least {{c1::90 percent}} of their taxable income for the year.
notes.explanation: The SEC notes this can mean regular dividends that income-seekers like.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Publicly Traded REITs
notes.evidence: REITs have to distribute at least 90 percent of their taxable income for the year.

notes.front: Why do REIT investments avoid double taxation?
notes.back: Income distributed to investors is not taxed at the entity level, only when investors receive and report it.
notes.explanation: A typical operating company, by contrast, is taxed before paying dividends.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Publicly Traded REITs
notes.evidence: For REITs, the income that is distributed to investors is not taxed at the entity level. Rather, that income is only subject to tax when investors receive the REIT distribution and report the income personally.

notes.front: How are REIT dividends generally taxed to shareholders?
notes.back: As ordinary income, without the reduced rates on other corporate dividends.
notes.explanation: Shareholders also pay tax on capital gains from the investment.
notes.evidence: Dividends paid by REITs generally are treated as ordinary income and are not entitled to the reduced tax rates on other types of corporate dividends.

notes.front: Publicly traded REIT vs non-traded REIT: which is listed on an exchange, and which is typically liquid?
notes.back: The publicly traded REIT: it is listed and typically liquid; the non-traded REIT is neither.
notes.explanation: Both are SEC-registered and file regular reports.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Non-traded REITs (31 August 2015)
notes.evidence: Publicly traded REITs (also called exchange-traded REITs ) are registered with the SEC, file regular reports with the SEC and are listed on an exchange such as the NYSE or NASDAQ.

notes.front: How do private REITs differ from non-traded REITs?
notes.back: Both are unlisted, but private REITs do not regularly file disclosure reports with the SEC; their offerings are private placements.
notes.explanation: This can make it hard to stay informed about the investment.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Non-traded REITs (31 August 2015)
notes.evidence: Similar to non-traded REITs, private REITs are not listed making them hard to value and trade. Private REITs also do not regularly file disclosure reports with the SEC possibly making it difficult for you to keep informed of your investment. Instead, private REIT offerings are private placements

notes.front: How do non-traded REIT investors usually get their money out?
notes.back: Generally by waiting for the REIT to list on an exchange or liquidate, which may take more than 10 years; early redemption programs are limited.
notes.explanation: Such programs may be discontinued or require a discount.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Non-traded REITs (31 August 2015)
notes.evidence: investors generally must wait until the non-traded REIT lists its shares on an exchange or liquidates its assets to achieve liquidity. These liquidity events, however, might not occur until more than 10 years after your investment.

notes.front: How high can non-traded REIT upfront fees run?
notes.back: Up to 15 percent of the offering price.
notes.explanation: The fees pay the firm or person selling the shares and cover the REIT’s offering and organisational costs, leaving less money to invest.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Non-traded REITs (31 August 2015)
notes.evidence: These fees can represent up to 15 percent of the offering price, which lowers the value and return of your investment and leaves less money for the REIT to invest.

notes.front: A client may need to sell her REIT shares at short notice. Which type suits her best?
notes.back: A: a publicly traded REIT.
notes.choices:
A) A publicly traded REIT
B) A non-traded REIT
C) A private REIT
notes.choicesExplained: B: non-traded REITs are illiquid. C: private REITs are also unlisted and hard to trade.
notes.explanation: An exchange listing makes publicly traded REITs typically liquid.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Non-traded REITs (31 August 2015)
notes.evidence: As with stocks listed on an exchange, you can buy and sell a publicly traded REIT with relative ease. An investment in publicly traded REITs is typically a liquid investment.

notes.front: Mortgage REITs vs REITs focused on properties: which tend to be more leveraged?
notes.back: Mortgage REITs, which lend to property owners directly or through mortgage-backed securities.
notes.explanation: Many also use derivatives and hedging to manage rate and credit exposure.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Publicly Traded REITs
notes.evidence: Mortgage REITs provide money to real estate owners and operators either directly in the form of mortgages or other types of real estate loans, or indirectly through the acquisition of mortgage-backed securities. Mortgage REITs tend to be more leveraged (that is, they use more borrowed capital) than REITs that are focused on properties.

notes.front: A REIT earns most of its income from mortgage loans to property owners and from mortgage-backed securities. What type is it?
notes.back: A: a mortgage REIT.
notes.choices:
A) A mortgage REIT
B) An equity (property) REIT
C) A direct participation program
notes.choicesExplained: B: an equity REIT focuses on owning properties. C: REITs are expressly excluded from the direct participation program definition.
notes.explanation: Mortgage REITs provide money to real estate owners and operators.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Publicly Traded REITs
notes.evidence: There are also REITs that invest in mortgages. Mortgage REITs provide money to real estate owners and operators either directly in the form of mortgages or other types of real estate loans

notes.front: Who can invest in a hedge fund?
notes.back: Depending on its structure, accredited investors or qualified purchasers, who meet income, asset or professional criteria.
notes.explanation: Hedge funds are not marketed to retail investors.
notes.evidence: You must be an accredited investor or a qualified purchaser. Depending on how the fund is structured, you will need to be an accredited investor or qualified purchaser to invest in hedge funds.

notes.front: How do hedge funds typically limit redemptions?
notes.back: To four times a year or fewer, often after a lock-up of one year or more; they may charge fees or suspend redemptions.
notes.explanation: Their holdings may be hard to sell and to value.
notes.evidence: Hedge funds typically limit opportunities to redeem, or cash in, your shares to four times a year or fewer. They also often impose a lock-up period of one year or more, during which you cannot cash in your shares.

notes.front: What fees do hedge fund investors typically pay?
notes.back: An asset management fee of 1–2% of NAV, plus a performance fee of 15–20% of profits.
notes.explanation: The SEC notes a performance fee could motivate a manager to take greater risks.
notes.evidence: Investors in hedge funds typically pay an asset management fee of 1-2% of NAV. In addition, they also typically pay a performance fee of 15-20% of the hedge fund’s profit

notes.front: What are two practices hedge funds use that mutual funds do not often use?
notes.back: Leverage and short-selling (among other speculative practices).
notes.explanation: Hedge funds typically have more flexible strategies than mutual funds.
notes.evidence: Many hedge funds seek to profit in all kinds of markets by using leverage (in other words, borrowing to increase investment exposure as well as risk), short-selling and other speculative investment practices that are not often used by mutual funds.

notes.front: Hedge fund vs mutual fund: which must redeem shares daily at NAV and meet disclosure and leverage limits?
notes.back: The mutual fund; hedge funds are not subject to those rules, though anti-fraud rules and managers’ fiduciary duty still apply.
notes.explanation: Hedge funds are not marketed to retail investors.
notes.evidence: They are not subject to the numerous regulations that apply to mutual funds and ETFs for the protection of investors—including requiring that mutual fund shares be redeemable on a daily basis based on the net asset value (NAV) ; protecting against conflicts of interest; ensuring fairness in the pricing of fund shares; requiring disclosure; limiting the use of leverage

notes.front: A retail client with modest savings may need cash within months and wants a hedge fund. What is the main obstacle besides eligibility?
notes.back: A: redemption limits and lock-ups.
notes.choices:
A) Redemption limits and lock-ups of a year or more
B) Daily redemption at NAV
C) Hedge funds pay no fees
notes.choicesExplained: B: daily redemption at NAV is a mutual fund feature hedge funds lack. C: hedge funds typically charge management and performance fees.
notes.explanation: Hedge funds often lock investors in and limit redemptions.
notes.evidence: They also often impose a lock-up period of one year or more, during which you cannot cash in your shares.

notes.front: What is a typical private equity fund strategy?
notes.back: Taking a controlling interest in an operating company and actively managing it to increase its value.
notes.explanation: Other private equity funds make minority investments in fast-growing companies or start-ups.
notes.evidence: A typical investment strategy undertaken by private equity funds is to take a controlling interest in an operating company or business—the portfolio company —and engage actively in the management and direction of the company or business in order to increase its value.

notes.front: Who can typically invest in a private equity fund, and in what legal role?
notes.back: Accredited investors and qualified clients, entering agreements as limited partners of the fund.
notes.explanation: The initial investment amount is often very high.
notes.evidence: A private equity fund is typically open only to accredited investors and qualified clients .

notes.front: What are the three types of exchange-traded product that Investor.gov lists?
notes.back: Exchange-traded funds; exchange-traded commodity trusts; exchange-traded notes.
notes.explanation: ETFs are the most common type.
notes.evidence: These investment products include exchange-traded funds, exchange-traded commodity trusts and exchange-traded notes (ETNs).

notes.front: ETF vs mutual fund: where and at what price do investors buy and sell shares?
notes.back: ETF: on national securities exchanges at market prices. Mutual fund: from or to the fund at the next calculated NAV.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov adds ETFs can sometimes be more tax efficient.
notes.evidence: unlike mutual funds, investors buy and sell ETF shares on national securities exchanges at market prices. In addition, ETFs can sometimes be more tax efficient than mutual funds.

notes.front: Can an ETF’s market price differ from its NAV?
notes.back: Yes: it may trade at a premium or discount to NAV, so buyers may pay more or less than NAV.
notes.explanation: ETF shares trade at market prices on exchanges.
notes.evidence: For a variety of reasons, an ETF’s market price may reflect a premium or a discount to the ETF’s underlying value or NAV. Therefore, an investor may pay more or less than the NAV when buying shares or receive more or less than NAV when selling shares.

notes.front: Why do many ETFs typically have fewer capital gains distributions than mutual funds?
notes.back: Many buy and sell portfolio securities through in-kind exchanges rather than for cash.
notes.explanation: Fewer distributions mean lower taxes.
notes.evidence: Because many ETFs buy and sell portfolio securities in in-kind exchange (rather than for cash), they typically have fewer capital gains distributions – and thus lower taxes – than mutual funds.

notes.front: An investor wants a diversified fund she can sell at market prices at any time the market is open. Which fits?
notes.back: A: an ETF.
notes.choices:
A) An ETF
B) A mutual fund
C) A non-traded REIT
notes.choicesExplained: B: mutual fund shares are redeemed with the fund at the next calculated NAV, not traded at market prices. C: non-traded REITs are illiquid.
notes.explanation: ETF investors can trade on the market whenever it is open.
notes.evidence: ETF investors can trade their shares on the market at the market price whenever the market is open—minus any fees.

notes.front: Why are ETN holders exposed to the issuer’s creditworthiness?
notes.back: Unlike ETFs, ETNs own no underlying portfolio of assets; holders are creditors if the issuer defaults.
notes.explanation: This is the fundamental difference the SEC draws between ETNs and ETFs.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Exchange Traded Notes (ETNs) (1 December 2015)
notes.evidence: Unlike ETFs, ETNs do not own an underlying portfolio of assets and this makes holders of ETNs subject to the creditworthiness of the issuer.

notes.front: ETNs generally {{c1::do not pay interest}}; their return is based on a reference index or benchmark, minus fees.
notes.explanation: This is how they differ from traditional corporate bonds.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Exchange Traded Notes (ETNs) (1 December 2015)
notes.evidence: the return on an ETN is based on the performance of a reference index or benchmark (minus any investor fees you may pay). ETNs generally do not pay interest to their holders.

notes.front: What are two fees an ETN buyer should consider?
notes.back: Any two of: fees in the reference index; daily investor fees reducing indicative value; brokerage commissions.
notes.explanation: The SEC lists these among ETN fee considerations.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Exchange Traded Notes (ETNs) (1 December 2015)
notes.evidence: What fees are associated with an ETN, such as fees included in the reference index or benchmark, daily investor fees that reduce the closing indicative value of the ETN, and the amount of brokerage commissions you may pay when buying and selling an ETN.

notes.front: An exchange-traded product is a bank’s unsecured debt, owns no portfolio and pays the return of a commodity index. What is it?
notes.back: B: an ETN.
notes.choices:
A) An ETF
B) An ETN
C) A UIT
notes.choicesExplained: A: an ETF owns an underlying portfolio of assets. C: a UIT is an investment company holding a fixed portfolio.
notes.explanation: ETNs are unsecured debt obligations linked to a reference index.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Exchange Traded Notes (ETNs) (1 December 2015)
notes.evidence: ETNs are unsecured debt obligations of financial institutions. They are very different from traditional corporate bonds

notes.front: Index fund vs actively managed fund: which usually has lower trading costs, better tax consequences and lower fees?
notes.back: The index fund, because passive management usually means less trading.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov says higher fees can significantly lower returns over time.
notes.evidence: Passive management usually translates into less trading of the fund’s portfolio (lower transaction costs), more favorable income tax consequences (lower realized capital gains), and lower fees and expenses than actively managed funds.

notes.front: Why may an index fund not perfectly match its index?
notes.back: Tracking error, for example from holding only a sample of the index; fees and trading costs can also cause underperformance.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov lists these among index fund risks.
notes.evidence: Tracking Error. An index fund may not perfectly track its index. For example, a fund may only invest in a sampling of the securities in the market index, in which case the fund’s performance may be less likely to match the index.

notes.front: An investor wants to match the S&P 500’s return, before fees, at low cost. Which fits?
notes.back: A: an index fund.
notes.choices:
A) An index fund
B) An actively managed fund
C) A hedge fund
notes.choicesExplained: B: an active fund tries to beat, not match, a benchmark and usually costs more. C: a hedge fund uses flexible, speculative strategies.
notes.explanation: An index fund aims for approximately the index’s return before fees.
notes.evidence: These funds follow a passive investment strategy designed to achieve approximately the same return as a particular index before fees.

notes.front: An investor compares Class A and Class C shares of the same fund. What differs between them?
notes.back: B: fees and expenses, and therefore performance.
notes.choices:
A) The investments held
B) The fees and expenses, and so performance
C) The investment objective
notes.choicesExplained: A: all classes hold identical investments. C: all classes share the same objectives and policies.
notes.explanation: Only the fee and expense structure separates the classes.
notes.evidence: All classes of a fund hold identical investments and have the same investment objectives and policies. But each class has different fees and expenses, and therefore, each class will have different performance results.

notes.front: A mutual fund pays, out of fund assets, for advertising and for compensating the brokers who sell its shares. What is this charge?
notes.back: A: a 12b-1 distribution fee.
notes.choices:
A) A 12b-1 distribution fee
B) A front-end load
C) A surrender charge
notes.choicesExplained: B: a front-end load is paid by the investor at purchase, not out of fund assets. C: a surrender charge applies to early variable annuity withdrawals.
notes.explanation: 12b-1 fees come out of fund assets to cover distribution costs.
notes.evidence: Distribution fees cover the marketing and selling of fund shares, such as compensating brokers and others who sell fund shares. These fees also pay for advertising, printing and mailing prospectuses to new investors, and for printing and mailing sales literature.

notes.front: In 2026, a 529 plan pays $8,000 of a beneficiary’s private high school tuition. How are the earnings withdrawn treated federally?
notes.back: A: tax-free, as a qualified expense within the $20,000 annual limit.
notes.choices:
A) Tax-free: it is a qualified expense within the $20,000 annual limit
B) Taxable: only college costs qualify
C) Deductible as a contribution
notes.choicesExplained: B: from 2026 up to $20,000 a year of elementary or secondary school expenses qualifies. C: 529 contributions are not deductible, and this is a withdrawal.
notes.explanation: Earnings used for qualified education expenses are not subject to federal tax.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. 529(e)(3)(A), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, section 70413(b)
notes.evidence: with respect to a beneficiary during any taxable year shall, in the aggregate, include not more than $20,000 in expenses described in subsection (c)(7) incurred during the taxable year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 26 U.S.C. 529 as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (taxable years from 2026)

notes.front: A REIT has $100 million of taxable income for the year. At least how much must it distribute?
notes.back: $90 million (at least 90 percent).
notes.explanation: The minimum is a share of taxable income: 90 percent of $100 million.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Publicly Traded REITs
notes.evidence: REITs have to distribute at least 90 percent of their taxable income for the year.

notes.front: An ETN charges a daily investor fee. What does that fee do?
notes.back: A: it reduces the closing indicative value.
notes.choices:
A) Reduces the ETN’s closing indicative value
B) Is paid by the issuer to holders
C) Only applies at maturity
notes.choicesExplained: B: investor fees are charged to holders, not paid to them. C: a daily fee applies each day.
notes.explanation: The SEC lists daily investor fees among ETN costs to weigh.
notes.source: SEC Investor Bulletin: Exchange Traded Notes (ETNs) (1 December 2015)
notes.evidence: daily investor fees that reduce the closing indicative value of the ETN
